Mild posterior subcapsular cataract visible in the affected eye at 7 weeks
key_facts: Patient is a white woman in her 20s
Unremarkable medical and ocular history
Symptoms began 4 days prior to presentation
Struck by lightning directly to the right forehead
Uncorrected visual acuity measured 20/50 OD and 20/20 OS
Pupils were symmetric, with no relative afferent pupillary defect
Initial anterior segment examination was normal
Initial dilated fundus examination showed no apparent abnormalities in either eye
Subtle irregularity of the outer retinal layers on initial OCT examination
Intraretinal cystoid changes and subfoveal ellipsoid zone disruption on OCT at 2 weeks
Restoration of foveal contour with decreased cystoid abnormalities on OCT at 7 weeks

rejected.label: Traumatic optic neuropathy

rejected.label: Lightning-induced cataract

rejected.label: Traumatic cataract
rejected.why: The cataract is likely a result of the electrical injury, not just a traumatic cataract

rejected.label: Traumatic optic neuropathy
rejected.why: There is no evidence of optic nerve damage or relative afferent pupillary defect

s1.syndrome_frame: Abdominal pain and constipation with a tender midline abdominal mass and history of amenorrhea
salient_findings: Tender midline abdominal mass
Amenorrhea for 3-4 months
Abdominal fullness and constipation
Undetectable thyroid-stimulating hormone
Elevated serum hCG
key_facts: 40-year-old woman
Presenting with abdominal pain and constipation
History of thyroid condition
Previously evaluated for amenorrhea
Thyroid-stimulating hormone was undetectable 3 months earlier
Prescribed methimazole
Continued to have amenorrhea
Reported abdominal fullness and constipation
Vital signs were unremarkable
Physical examination revealed a tender midline abdominal mass
Point-of-care urine hCG test was negative
Serum hCG was 74,503 mIU/mL
Ultrasonography confirmed live intrauterine pregnancy at 24 weeks

raw.rationale: Ultrasonography confirmed live intrauterine pregnancy at 24 weeks, which explains the abdominal pain, constipation, and abdominal fullness, and is consistent with the high serum hCG level

rejected.label: Molar pregnancy
rejected.why: Typically presents with abnormally high hCG levels and ultrasonographic findings of a heterogeneous mass, not a live intrauterine pregnancy

rejected.label: Uterine leiomyoma
rejected.why: May cause abdominal pain and constipation, but would not explain the high serum hCG level or the live intrauterine pregnancy on ultrasonography

rejected.label: Ovarian tumor
rejected.why: Would not explain the live intrauterine pregnancy on ultrasonography or the high serum hCG level

rejected.label: Placenta accreta
rejected.why: Is a complication of pregnancy, but the ultrasonography findings do not suggest placenta accreta, and the presentation is more consistent with a normal intrauterine pregnancy

s1.syndrome_frame: Acute coronary syndrome with recurrent chest pain and electrocardiographic changes
salient_findings: Paroxysmal chest pain occurring 5 times during the day
Elevated cardiac troponin I level
ST-segment elevation in leads III and aVR on initial ECG
key_facts: Patient presented to the emergency department with chest pain
Chest pain was paroxysmal and occurred 5 times during the day
Each episode of chest pain lasted 15 to 30 minutes
Blood pressure was 106/52 mm Hg
Pulse rate was 64 beats per minute
Chest auscultation revealed normal breath and heart sounds with no murmurs
Hemogram, serum electrolyte levels, kidney and liver function tests, B-type natriuretic peptide and D-dimer levels were all within normal limits
Cardiac troponin I level was elevated at 25 ng/mL
Initial ECG revealed sinus rhythm, ST-segment elevation in leads III and aVR, Q wave in lead III, and ST-segment depression in leads I, II, aVL, aVF, and V2 to V6
Repeated ECG showed sinus bradycardia, Q-wave amplitude deepening, ST-segment falling back to equipotential line, and T-wave inversion in lead III
Coronary angiography showed total occlusion of the right coronary artery and subtotal occlusion of the left main coronary artery

shortlist.label: Acute myocardial infarction
shortlist.why_kept: Elevated cardiac troponin I level and total occlusion of the right coronary artery

shortlist.label: Unstable angina
shortlist.why_kept: Recurrent chest pain and electrocardiographic changes with subtotal occlusion of the left main coronary artery

shortlist.label: Variant angina

shortlist.why_kept: ST-segment elevation and recurrent chest pain, potentially indicative of vasospastic angina

raw.rationale: Elevated cardiac troponin I level and ECG changes including ST-segment elevation and Q wave in lead III, along with total occlusion of the right coronary artery on coronary angiography, are indicative of acute myocardial infarction.

rejected.label: Unstable angina
rejected.why: Unstable angina typically does not present with elevated troponin levels or significant ECG changes like Q waves and ST-segment elevation.

rejected.label: Variant angina
rejected.why: Variant angina is characterized by chest pain at rest with transient ST-segment elevation, but it does not typically cause elevated troponin levels or Q waves on ECG.

rejected.label: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection
rejected.why: While possible, the information provided does not specifically suggest dissection, and the findings are more consistent with acute myocardial infarction due to occlusion.

rejected.label: Coronary artery spasm
rejected.why: Coronary artery spasm could cause chest pain and some ECG changes, but the presence of elevated troponin, Q waves, and total occlusion of a coronary artery points more towards an acute myocardial infarction.

s1.syndrome_frame: Recurrent unilateral neck cellulitis with associated temporal bone anomalies and fistula
salient_findings: Unilateral otomandibular syndrome with severe temporal bone hypoplasia
Recurrent deep unilateral neck cellulitis
Discharge through the artificial ear canal during episodes of cellulitis
Fistula originating from the middle ear
key_facts: Patient is a man in his 40s
History of unilateral otomandibular syndrome
Severe temporal bone hypoplasia
Multiple mandibular and auricular reconstruction surgeries in childhood
First episode of neck cellulitis occurred in 2014
Second episode of neck cellulitis occurred in 2021
Discharge through the artificial ear canal during the second episode
Recurrence of neck cellulitis two months after the second episode
Imaging studies showed collection in the right parapharyngeal space and neck
Hypodense lesion noted in the middle ear on initial CT scan
Fistula originating from the middle ear on follow-up MRI
2-centimeter mass found during drilling of the hypoplastic petrous bone
Millimetric fistula at the tip of the mastoid running into the sternocleidomastoid muscle

shortlist.label: First branchial cleft anomaly
shortlist.why_kept: Associated with recurrent neck cellulitis and temporal bone anomalies

shortlist.label: Cholesteatoma
shortlist.why_kept: Middle ear mass and fistula are consistent with cholesteatoma complications

shortlist.label: Temporal bone osteomyelitis
shortlist.why_kept: Severe temporal bone hypoplasia and recurrent infections suggest chronic osteomyelitis

shortlist.label: Mastoiditis
shortlist.why_kept: Inflammation of the mastoid bone is consistent with the patient's symptoms and imaging findings

shortlist.label: Fistula of the middle ear
shortlist.why_kept: Directly observed on imaging studies and consistent with the patient's discharge through the artificial ear canal

raw.rationale: The patient's history of unilateral otomandibular syndrome, severe temporal bone hypoplasia, and recurrent neck cellulitis with discharge through the artificial ear canal, along with imaging findings of a fistula originating from the middle ear and a millimetric fistula at the tip of the mastoid, are consistent with a first branchial cleft anomaly.

rejected.label: Cholesteatoma
rejected.why: While cholesteatoma could explain the middle ear findings, it does not fully account for the patient's history of unilateral otomandibular syndrome and severe temporal bone hypoplasia.

rejected.label: Temporal bone osteomyelitis
rejected.why: Osteomyelitis could be a complication of the patient's condition, but it does not explain the underlying cause of the recurrent neck cellulitis and fistulae.

rejected.label: Mastoiditis
rejected.why: Mastoiditis is a possible complication, but the patient's symptoms and imaging findings suggest a more complex congenital anomaly.

rejected.label: Fistula of the middle ear
rejected.why: While a fistula of the middle ear is present, it is likely a component of the larger congenital anomaly, rather than the primary diagnosis itself.

s1.syndrome_frame: Chronic mucocutaneous blistering disorder with oral and skin involvement
salient_findings: Intractable mucocutaneous lesions for 10 years
Presence of bullae, erosions, and crusts on the lower lip, oral cavity, face, trunk, and extremities
Skin biopsy showing spongiosis, neutrophils, and perivascular dermatitis
key_facts: 39-year-old woman with no significant medical history
No swollen cervical and axillary lymph nodes
Small bullae, erosions, and crusts on the lower lip
Erosions with epithelized mucosa in the oral cavity
Flaccid discrete and coalesced bullae, crusts, and erosions on the face, trunk, and extremities
Normal chest, abdomen, and pelvic computed tomography
Normal gastrointestinal endoscopy and colonoscopy results
Skin biopsy revealed spongiosis and numerous neutrophils with nuclear dust in the epidermis
Superficial perivascular dermatitis with predominant infiltration of lymphocytes in the dermis
Positive immunoblotting for IgG autoantibodies to envoplakin and periplakin

shortlist.label: Paraneoplastic pemphigus
shortlist.why_kept: Positive immunoblotting for IgG autoantibodies to envoplakin and periplakin, which is characteristic of paraneoplastic pemphigus

shortlist.label: Mucous membrane pemphigoid
shortlist.why_kept: Chronic mucocutaneous blistering disorder with oral and skin involvement, consistent with mucous membrane pemphigoid

shortlist.label: Pemphigus vulgaris
shortlist.why_kept: Presence of mucocutaneous lesions and positive immunoblotting, although the lack of IgG antibodies to Dsg1 and Dsg3 makes it less likely

shortlist.label: Linear IgA bullous dermatosis
shortlist.why_kept: Chronic blistering disorder with linear IgA deposits, although the negative direct IF results make it less likely

shortlist.label: Lichen planus pemphigoides
shortlist.why_kept: Interface dermatitis and presence of mucocutaneous lesions, although the lack of specific immunological findings makes it less likely

raw.rationale: The presence of autoantibodies to envoplakin and periplakin, as well as the clinical presentation of mucocutaneous lesions, is most consistent with paraneoplastic pemphigus.

rejected.label: Mucous membrane pemphigoid
rejected.why: Lack of deposits of IgG, IgA, and C3 at the basement membrane zone and negative indirect IF using 1-molar sodium chloride-split normal human skin

rejected.label: Pemphigus vulgaris
rejected.why: Negative chemiluminescent enzyme immunoassays for Dsg1 and Dsg3

rejected.label: Linear IgA bullous dermatosis
rejected.why: Negative direct IF for IgA deposits and lack of linear IgA deposits at the basement membrane zone

rejected.label: Lichen planus pemphigoides
rejected.why: Clinical and histopathological features do not align with lichen planus pemphigoides, and the presence of autoantibodies to envoplakin and periplakin is more specific for paraneoplastic pemphigus
